articleHeadline: Meningococcal meningitis: understand the risks, symptoms, and the importance of vaccination.
articleSummary: Meningococcal meningitis, caused by Neisseria meningitidis, is a medical emergency requiring rapid diagnosis and hospitalization. While any age can be affected, higher incidence occurs in children, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals. Seasonality peaks in winter and spring, when crowded indoor environments facilitate transmission. Early warning signs include fever above 38°C, severe headache, nausea/vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, drowsiness, and purpuric skin rashes; in infants, persistent crying, irritability, stiff body, seizures, and a tense fontanelle warrant urgent pediatric evaluation. Diagnosis relies on lumbar puncture with CSF analysis; treatment is immediate IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime), with ICU support for septic shock. Vaccination is the most effective prevention and is part of the basic baby immunization schedule; close contacts may require post-exposure antibiotic prophylaxis. articleHeadline: In a Drier World, Some Infectious Diseases are Unexpectedly Thriving
articleSummary: Dry conditions linked to drought-disease paradox reveal water-borne pathogens can surge as ponds dry. A Trends in Ecology and Evolution paper synthesizes ~100 studies across humans, wildlife, and insects, showing drought often boosts diseases such as cholera, West Nile virus, and dengue, while sometimes suppressing others like some pathogens in hot, low-oxygen waters. In California during 2000s droughts, valley fever cases rose; a 2014 drought coincided with a West Nile virus spike. Somalia’s 2017 drought saw nearly 80,000 cholera cases and more than 1,000 deaths. In Brazil, dengue risk increases months after drought. A wildlife-focused mechanism: during drought, waterholes shrink, animals crowd together, fecal matter concentrates parasites; Titcomb’s review notes >100,000 parasite eggs per kilogram of dung after drought. Globally, the world is ~77% drier than three decades ago, amplifying opportunities for disease spread alongside rising temperatures.

articleHeadline: The Bubonic Plague Outbreak Is Still Deadly, Like in the Middle Ages.
articleSummary: Bubonic plague, caused by Yersinia pestis, remains deadly with Madagascar as the current hotspot, affecting about 250–500 people annually out of roughly 3,000 global cases per year per the Robert Koch Institute. The disease persists in Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda, and occasionally in western United States (Oregon). It presents in three forms: bubonic (lymph node swelling, flea transmission from infected rodents), pneumonic (airborne, capable of human-to-human spread), and septicemic (bacteria in the bloodstream). Pneumonic plague is the only form primarily transmissible between people. Historically, Europe’s medieval pandemic (1347–1353) killed about 25 million people, roughly 60% of the population. Yersinia pestis has ancient origins, detected in remains over 5,500 years old; a late-medieval shift enabled flea-based transmission. Europe has been plague-free since 1945, with last cases on Corsica. The article references researchers Krause-Kyora and Holger Scholz of the Robert Koch Institute.
